facts.value: The subject of Egyptology and Coptology is the knowledge of the culture of Pharaonic and Christian Egypt in all its facets.
The field covers the period from the merging of various Neolithic cultures in the northern Nile Valley in the 4th millennium BCE to the Christian-Coptic era.
The period after the Arab conquest of Egypt (640/641 CE) is covered by Oriental Studies and Semitic Studies.
The geographical scope of Egyptology encompasses the territory of today's Arab Republic of Egypt as well as the northern part of the Republic of Sudan.

The special relevance of Egyptology as a scientific discipline lies in its wide range, encompassing the entire social system of one of humanity's earliest advanced civilizations over more than four millennia.
Egyptology offers many interesting points of connection for the modern world with its increasingly complex intercultural relations.
Egyptology increasingly integrates numerous seemingly divergent cultural and natural scientific disciplines into an optimal overall concept.

facts.value: The programme imparts humanities and cultural studies competence.

Key qualifications to ensure employability outside the subject area are taught, including exercises in rhetoric, didactics, academic writing, foreign language competence, and the ability to give public presentations.
Career prospects within the field are limited.
Employment opportunities are available in the areas of museums, universities, and excavation archaeology.

Students are advised not to wait until shortly before or after their first academic degree to start career orientation; instead, they should make career orientation a project that accompanies their entire studies from the first semesters onward.
Numerous career tips are provided, which students can approach step by step during their studies or select those that seem relevant and useful to them.
The university charges the basic fee and the solidarity contribution for the semester ticket for the Munich Student Union.

facts.value: Archaeological fieldwork using the latest techniques.
Philological elucidation of one of the oldest writing and language systems.
Art historical recording and evaluation of the self-expression of early human civilization.
Development of a comprehensive historical perspective through the analysis of written and archaeological documents.
Research into one of the earliest religious systems that had an impact on Christianity, Judaism, and Islam.
Discovery of intercultural relations between Egypt and its neighbors in the Near East and Africa.
Reconstruction of a diverse landscape history of a cultural region shaped for thousands of years.

Integration of natural sciences as archaeometric auxiliary sciences, including: geology and petrology, geophysics, anthropology, and various biological sub-disciplines up to and including modern DNA analyses and palaeozoology.
Students must acquire a large part of the knowledge on their own, as only partial aspects of a specific field or topic can be addressed in the courses.
Students are led to independent research activities at a very early stage, for example in the preparation of presentations.
